The question of whether humans possess innate knowledge is one of the most enduring debates in philosophy and cognitive science, with strongly opposing camps. On one side, rationalist philosophers and modern researchers argue that we do have innate knowledge. Plato, Descartes, and Leibniz all maintained that humans are born with certain ideas — particularly mathematical truisms — that are triggered by experience rather than derived from it [d1]. Modern psychological and evolutionary research supports this: the human brain is said to possess innate knowledge such as the understanding that three-dimensional objects persist when not observed, knowledge acquired through evolution [d2]. Researchers like Noam Chomsky and Northeastern professor Iris Berent argue that language intuition is inborn, and Berent's studies show that people are actually cognitively biased against accepting innate knowledge despite evidence for it [d3]. Scientific American reports that researchers have argued there is "no longer a serious alternative" to the view that humans have an innate capacity to process numbers, though critics and a new wave of empiricism have emerged to challenge this [d5].

On the opposing side, John Locke's empiricist tradition flatly rejects innate knowledge. Locke argued that the mind at birth is a tabula rasa — a blank slate — and that all knowledge is acquired solely through sensory experience [d6][d9]. In his own words, Locke contended it is self-contradictory to claim we have innate knowledge we are unaware of, saying such a view amounts to saying "that men know, and know them not, at the same time" [d7]. This empiricist position holds that even mathematical truths are based solely on experience, not on inborn ideas [d8]. The innate knowledge thesis, as described by rationalists, asserts knowledge whose source is our own nature and which does not depend on experience for justification [d4], but Locke and his followers deny this entirely [d9].
